To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the combination of systemic antibiotics and “lock therapy” can be used in the treatment of multiresistant Gram- negative infections, such as S. maltophilia sepses, in cancer patients with CVCs in situ.

(i) S. maltophilia is an emerging pathogen, especially among cancer patients, (ii) the use of systemic antibiotic therapy associated to “lock therapy” can be effective for treating S. maltophilia infections, and (iii) the surveillance of CVC is the cornerstone for the prevention of CVC-related sepsis.

1) S. maltophilia infections are rare but can be life-threatening, particularly when they occur in patients with compromised immune systems; 2) CVC-related infections are the most frequent type of S. maltophilia infection in hospitalized patients; 3) CVC lock therapy can be a useful tool in the treatment of S. maltophila infections.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the role played by the CVC in the pathogenesis of sepsis, and the possibility to prevent and treat it by the use of a “lock” solution.
the prevention of nosocoial infections, in order to improve patients' safety.
the study of the molecular basis of the pathogenesis of bacterial infections, and the development of new therapeutic approaches.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“the prevention of CVC-related infections should be considered a priority, in order to avoid the spread of nosocomial pathogens, and to prevent the emergence of new resistant strains”.
“the prevention is better than the cure”.
the combination of systemic and lock therapy represents a valid option in the treatment of CVC-related sepsis, caused by multiresistant Gramnegative rods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
“good practice”, in association with a multidisciplinary approach, can be a successful tool for the prevention of these infections.
“the best way to prevent a septicemia is to avoid the insertion of a CVC”.
“good practice” and a multidisciplinary approach are essential to prevent and treat infections caused by multiresistant Gramnegative rods.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the combination of systemic antibiotic therapy and lock therapy is an effective strategy for the management of CVC-related infections caused by multiresistant bacteria, allowing to save the in situ CVD.
the use of “lock therapy” is a safe and effective strategy to manage catheter-related infections in selected patients.
“lock therapy” is a safe and effective treatment for catheter related infections, and it can be considered an alternative to the removal of the catheter.
